headline: Give UK Your Data, Nobel Economist Tells Anthropic and OpenAI
author: Jacob Reid

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- The UK's fledgling AI Economics Institute is aiming for what its chairman calls the "holy grail:" linking data from companies and AI labs with everything the government knows about individuals and businesses.

Having all of that information — including tax records and the HMRC business register — will help the institute work out how artificial intelligence is actually changing the economy, according to Simon Johnson, the Nobel prize-winning economist who chairs it.

"You can have a level of detail and texture that nobody else has, including the big labs, because they don't have the administrative data," Johnson told Bloomberg. That will help his institute gauge "what's happening to total jobs, who's losing a job, who's gaining a job, how does this match up with skills and experience," he said.

The UK government is trying to understand how AI is altering the economy as ministers seek to avoid stifling the development of the quickly-advancing technology while managing the risks associated with it.

"The range of plausible economic outcomes from AI is wide," the government said in June, setting out the institute's role. "AI is widely expected to raise productivity, but evidence of firm-level or aggregate effects remains limited."

Johnson's institute was set up by the government to build the evidence base ministers need to inform policy decisions and is modeled directly on the UK's AI Security Institute, which has become the world leader in testing cutting edge models before they're released. Last month Britain also announced an AI Biosecurity Lab to detect and monitor biological threats.

AI labs including Anthropic PBC — which held an initial public offering on Thursday — and OpenAI, have been "very positive" about working with the institute and haven't yet turned down a request for data, Johnson said. They already publish some usage data, but it's generally aggregated and excludes enterprise accounts.
Neither Anthropic nor OpenAI responded to a request for comment.

Companies have also been "pretty open and thoughtful and candid" in confidentially sharing information about what they're using AI for and how tasks, roles and wages are changing, Johnson said. "Nobody is closing their ears, nobody says, 'Don't talk to me, I want to bury my head in the sand'."

The proliferation of institutes reflects the UK's broader approach to research, monitor and use the technology, rather than passing new regulations. Britain is trying to position itself as an "honest broker" on AI between the US, which has so far refrained from passing federal legislation, and the European Union, which quickly passed sweeping AI laws that are unpopular in the industry.

Explaining the similarities with the model-testing institute, Johnson said: "You have expertise, and you have some people who are established civil servants, and some people who are data nerds, and then you bring them together and you elevate them within Whitehall in such a way as they have access and they're available to answer questions."

AI helped the UK economy to grow at its fastest pace in two and a half years in the third quarter, Office for National Statistics data show. It will boost productivity by 0.2 percentage points a year in the medium term, according to the Office for Budget Responsibility, although it notes the scale and timing of that uplift is highly uncertain.
AI minister Kanishka Narayan has said how much the country adopts AI will be "the biggest driver" of whether the government has a surplus or needs to make cuts to meet its fiscal rules.

Johnson, who is from the UK but has lived in the US for 40 years, said the relationship between AI labs and the government is better in Britain. "This whole discussion or thinking around the social license to operate is much more salient here," he said. "And the EU is more on the lines of 'the answer is no, so what's the question?'"
